specStatements.text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable. The nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. This is a random process called radioactive decay.
Activity is the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decay s.
Activity is measured in becquerel (Bq)
Count-rate is the number of decays recorded each second by a detector (eg Geiger-Muller tube).
The nuclear radiation emitted may be:
• an alpha particle (α) – this consists of two neutrons and two protons, it is the same as a helium nucleus
• a beta particle (β) – a high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton
• a gamma ray (γ) – electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus
• a neutron (n).
Required knowledge of the properties of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays is limited to their penetration through materials, their range in air and ionising power.
Students should be able to apply their knowledge to the uses of radiation and evaluate the best sources of radiation to use in a given situation.
Nuclear equations are used to represent radioactive decay.
In a nuclear equation an alpha particle may be represented by the symbol:
and a beta particle by the symbol:
The emission of the different types of nuclear radiation may cause a change in the mass and /or the charge of the nucleus. For example:
So alpha decay causes both the mass and charge of the nucleus to decrease.
So beta decay does not cause the mass of the nucleus to change but does cause the charge of the nucleus to increase.
Students are not required to recall these two examples.

Students should be able to use the names and symbols of common nuclei and particles to write balanced equations that show single alpha (α) and beta (β) decay. This is limited to balancing the atomic numbers and mass numbers. The identification of daughter elements from such decays is not required.
The emission of a gamma ray does not cause the mass or the charge of the nucleus to change.
Radioactive decay is random.

The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve, or the time it takes for the count rate (or activity) from a sample containing the isotope to fall to half its initial level.
Students should be able to explain the concept of half-life and how it is related to the random nature of radioactive decay.
Students should be able to determine the half-life of a radioactive isotope from given information.
(HT only) Students should be able to calculate the net decline, expressed as a ratio, in a radioactive emission after a given number of half-lives.

Radioactive contamination is the unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials. The hazard from contamination is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms. The type of radiation emitted affects the level of hazard.
Irradiation is the process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation. The irradiated object does not become radioactive.
Students should be able to compare the hazards associated with contamination and irradiation.
Suitable precautions must be taken to protect against any hazard that the radioactive source used in the process of irradiation may present.

Students should understand that it is important for the findings of studies into the effects of radiation on humans to be published and shared with other scientists so that the findings can be checked by peer review.

scopeNotes.statement: Required knowledge of the properties of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays is limited to their penetration through materials, their range in air and ionising power.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only three properties are taught and tested for each radiation: what absorbs it, how far it travels in air, and how strongly it ionises. Nothing here asks about deflection in electric or magnetic fields, charge-to-mass ratios, decay energies or energy spectra, half-value thickness, absorption coefficients, or the biological mechanism by which ionisation damages a cell. Where a use of radiation is evaluated in q13-q15, the reasoning is built only from penetration, range in air and ionising power.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not required to recall these two examples.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks a student to reproduce the specification's own worked examples of alpha and beta decay from memory. Where a decay equation appears (q21), the parent nuclide and the symbol of the daughter are supplied in the stem, so the task is balancing numbers rather than recalling a named example.

scopeNotes.statement: This is limited to balancing the atomic numbers and mass numbers. The identification of daughter elements from such decays is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Balancing questions supply the chemical symbol of the daughter nucleus in the stem and ask only for the mass number and the atomic number. No item requires a student to work out which element is produced, to use a periodic table to name a daughter, or to recall decay chains or series.

concepts.definition: The process in which an unstable nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. It is a random process.
A nucleus that will give out radiation at some point because its present combination of protons and neutrons is not stable.
A process in which it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next, or when a particular nucleus will decay. Only the average behaviour of a large number of nuclei is predictable.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays.
The unit in which activity is measured. One becquerel is one decay each second.
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector. It is smaller than the activity of the source, because a detector only intercepts some of the radiation emitted.
A detector of nuclear radiation. Each particle or ray it absorbs produces a pulse, and the pulses are counted to give a count-rate.
The radiation emitted by an unstable nucleus. It may be an alpha particle, a beta particle, a gamma ray or a neutron.
A particle emitted from a nucleus consisting of two neutrons and two protons; it is the same as a helium nucleus.
A high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton.
Electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus.
The emission of a neutron from an unstable nucleus. It is one of the types of nuclear radiation listed by the specification.
How far radiation travels into a material before it is absorbed. Alpha is stopped by paper or skin, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma is only reduced by thick lead or concrete.
How far radiation travels through air before it is absorbed. Alpha travels a few centimetres, beta about a metre, and gamma travels a very long way.
How strongly radiation removes electrons from the atoms it passes. Alpha is the most ionising, beta is weaker, and gamma is the least ionising.
An equation used to represent radioactive decay, showing the parent nucleus on the left and the products of the decay on the right.
The top number in a nuclear symbol, giving the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. It must balance across a nuclear equation.
The bottom number in a nuclear symbol, giving the number of protons and therefore the charge of the nucleus. It must balance across a nuclear equation.
Alpha decay causes both the mass and the charge of the nucleus to decrease: the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.
Beta decay does not cause the mass of the nucleus to change but does cause the charge of the nucleus to increase: the atomic number rises by 1.
The emission of a gamma ray does not cause the mass or the charge of the nucleus to change.
Choosing the mass numbers and atomic numbers so that the total mass number and the total atomic number are the same on both sides of the equation.
The time it takes for the number of nuclei of an isotope in a sample to halve, or the time it takes for the count rate or activity from the sample to fall to half its initial level.
After n half-lives the emission has fallen by a factor of 2 to the power n, so the net decline is written as the ratio 1 : 2 to the power n.
The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials. The hazard is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms.
The process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation. The irradiated object does not become radioactive.

Steps such as handling a source with tongs, keeping it at a distance, limiting exposure time and storing it in a lead-lined container, taken to protect against any hazard the source used for irradiation may present.
The checking of published findings by other scientists. It is why studies of the effects of radiation on humans must be published and shared.

concepts.term: Choosing a source for a use
concepts.definition: Selecting the radiation whose penetration, range in air and ionising power suit the job: alpha where the radiation must be absorbed over a short distance, beta where it must pass through thin material, gamma where it must pass through thick material or out of a body.
In a nuclear equation an alpha particle may be represented by the symbol ⁴₂He, with mass number 4 written above and atomic number 2 below.
In a nuclear equation a beta particle is represented by the symbol ⁰₋₁e, with mass number 0 written above and charge −1 below.

misconceptions.question: Can you say when a particular unstable nucleus will decay?
misconceptions.correct: No. Decay is random, so neither which nucleus decays next nor when it decays can be predicted.
misconceptions.misconception: Each nucleus has a scheduled moment of decay that could be worked out if you knew enough about it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Half-life is quoted as a definite number and decay graphs are smooth, so decay looks like clockwork.
misconceptions.correction: The definite half-life is a statistical result from an enormous number of nuclei. A single nucleus only has a chance of decaying in the next second.

misconceptions.question: Is the count-rate the same as the activity of the source?
misconceptions.correct: No. Activity is the rate at which the nuclei in the source decay; count-rate is the number of decays a detector records each second.
misconceptions.misconception: A Geiger-Muller tube records every decay, so the count-rate is the activity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are quoted per second and both fall together, so the two numbers feel interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: The detector only intercepts radiation that happens to travel towards it and be absorbed, so the count-rate is always lower than the activity.

misconceptions.question: What quantity does the becquerel measure?
misconceptions.correct: Activity, in decays each second.
misconceptions.misconception: The becquerel measures the energy or the dose that the radiation delivers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radiation units are met together, and Bq is grouped with the units used for absorbed dose.
misconceptions.correction: The becquerel counts events: one becquerel is one decay each second. It says nothing about the energy carried.

misconceptions.question: Is an alpha particle a helium atom?
misconceptions.correct: No. It consists of two neutrons and two protons, so it is the same as a helium nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: An alpha particle is a whole helium atom, complete with two electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words 'helium nucleus' and the symbol ⁴₂He look like the helium already known from chemistry.
misconceptions.correction: Only the nucleus is emitted. There are no electrons in it, which is why an alpha particle carries a charge of +2.

misconceptions.question: Where does a beta particle come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the nucleus: it is a high speed electron ejected as a neutron turns into a proton.
misconceptions.misconception: A beta particle is an electron knocked out of one of the outer shells of the atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electrons are taught as shell particles, so an emitted electron is assumed to be a shell electron.
misconceptions.correction: The electron is created in the nucleus at the instant a neutron changes into a proton. That is why the atomic number rises.

misconceptions.question: Is a gamma ray a particle?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: A gamma ray is a small uncharged particle thrown out of the nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It is listed alongside alpha and beta particles, so it is assumed to be a particle too.
misconceptions.correction: Gamma is part of the electromagnetic spectrum. It has no mass and no charge, which is why gamma emission changes neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus.

misconceptions.question: Does nuclear radiation come from the electrons?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is emitted by the nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: Radiation is given out when electrons move between energy levels closer to the nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Light emission by electrons changing energy level is taught elsewhere and is transferred to radioactivity.
misconceptions.correction: Radioactive decay is a change in the nucleus. Nothing the electrons do can start it, stop it or alter its rate.

misconceptions.question: Which radiation is the most penetrating?
misconceptions.correct: Gamma. Alpha is the least penetrating and is stopped by paper or skin.
misconceptions.misconception: Alpha is the most penetrating because it is the biggest and heaviest of the radiations.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Being large and massive is read as being powerful, so the biggest particle is assumed to push furthest.
misconceptions.correction: Being large and highly charged makes alpha interact with almost every atom it meets, so it loses its energy within a few centimetres of air.

misconceptions.question: Which radiation is the most ionising?
misconceptions.correct: Alpha. Gamma is the least ionising.
misconceptions.misconception: Gamma is the most ionising because it is the most penetrating.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Penetration and ionising power are both treated as measures of how strong a radiation is, so they are assumed to rise together.
misconceptions.correction: They run in opposite directions. Gamma passes through matter precisely because it interacts with so few atoms on the way.

misconceptions.question: How far does an alpha particle travel in air?
misconceptions.correct: Only a few centimetres.
misconceptions.misconception: Alpha travels several metres through air, as beta and gamma do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All three are called radiation, so all three are assumed to reach across a room.
misconceptions.correction: Alpha ionises so strongly that it runs out of energy within a few centimetres. Beta travels about a metre and gamma travels much further.

misconceptions.question: Does lead stop gamma radiation completely?
misconceptions.correct: No. Thick lead or concrete reduces gamma radiation, but some always gets through.
misconceptions.misconception: A thin sheet of lead absorbs gamma radiation completely, the way paper absorbs alpha.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The absorber table is memorised as 'paper, aluminium, lead' with the same word 'stopped' used for all three rows.
misconceptions.correction: Gamma is only reduced by an absorber. The thicker the lead, the smaller the count-rate, but it never reaches zero.

misconceptions.question: Can heating a source change how fast it decays?
misconceptions.correct: No. The rate of decay is not affected by heating, pressure or chemical change.
misconceptions.misconception: Radioactive decay speeds up when the material is heated, as a chemical reaction does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other rate met in science, from dissolving to reacting, depends on temperature.
misconceptions.correction: Decay is a nuclear process. Heating changes only the motion of the atoms, and cannot reach the nucleus.

misconceptions.question: Can a nucleus emit a neutron?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A neutron (n) is one of the types of nuclear radiation the specification lists.
misconceptions.misconception: A nucleus cannot emit a neutron; anything uncharged coming out must be gamma, and anything else must be beta.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alpha, beta and gamma are drilled as 'the three radiations', so the fourth bullet is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists four possible emissions: alpha, beta, gamma and a neutron.

misconceptions.question: By how much does the mass number fall in alpha decay?
misconceptions.correct: By 4, and the atomic number falls by 2.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass number falls by 2, because two protons leave the nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Only the protons in the alpha particle are counted, and the two neutrons that also leave are forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: An alpha particle is two protons plus two neutrons, so four nucleons leave: mass number down 4, atomic number down 2.

misconceptions.question: Does the mass number change in beta decay?
misconceptions.correct: No. Beta decay does not cause the mass of the nucleus to change.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass number falls by 1 because a particle has left the nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Something leaving is expected to reduce the mass, and the neutron becoming a proton is not tracked.
misconceptions.correction: The electron has a mass number of 0, and the neutron that vanished has been replaced by a proton, so the count of nucleons is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: Does the charge of the nucleus fall in beta decay?
misconceptions.correct: No. Beta decay causes the charge of the nucleus to increase by 1.
misconceptions.misconception: The atomic number falls by 1 because a negatively charged particle has been lost.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Losing a negative particle sounds like losing charge, and the minus sign in ⁰₋₁e reinforces it.
misconceptions.correction: Losing a negative charge leaves the nucleus more positive. A neutron has become a proton, so the atomic number rises by 1.

misconceptions.question: Does gamma emission change the mass number?
misconceptions.correct: No. It changes neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: Emitting a gamma ray reduces the mass number, because something has been emitted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alpha and beta decay both change the numbers, so gamma is assumed to change them as well.
misconceptions.correction: A gamma ray has no mass number and no charge, so both numbers in the nuclear symbol stay the same.

misconceptions.question: How is an alpha particle written in a nuclear equation?
misconceptions.correct: As ⁴₂He, with mass number 4 above and atomic number 2 below.
misconceptions.misconception: It is written ²₄He, with the 2 above and the 4 below.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two numbers are learned as a pair without linking each to what it counts, so their positions are swapped.
misconceptions.correction: The top number is always the mass number. An alpha particle has 4 nucleons and 2 protons, so it is ⁴₂He.

misconceptions.question: What charge is written on a beta particle?
misconceptions.correct: −1, in the symbol ⁰₋₁e.
misconceptions.misconception: A beta particle is written with a charge of +1, or with a mass number of 1.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Beta decay is known to make the nucleus more positive, and the plus sign is attached to the beta particle itself.
misconceptions.correction: The beta particle is an electron, so its charge is −1 and its mass number is 0. It is the nucleus left behind whose charge rises.

misconceptions.question: What does a half-life of 6 hours mean?
misconceptions.correct: In 6 hours the number of nuclei, and the count rate, falls to half its starting value.
misconceptions.misconception: A half-life of 6 hours means the sample has fully decayed after 6 hours, or that it is half of the total decay time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'life' suggests a lifetime, so 'half-life' is read as a fraction of the time until the sample is finished.
misconceptions.correction: Half-life measures halving, not finishing. After each half-life whatever is left halves again, so there is always something left.

misconceptions.question: Is a sample completely decayed after two half-lives?
misconceptions.correct: No. A quarter of the original nuclei are still undecayed.
misconceptions.misconception: Two half-lives means two lots of a half, which uses up the whole sample.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Halves are added rather than applied one after the other, so 50% + 50% is taken to be 100%.
misconceptions.correction: The second half-life halves what is left, not the original. After two half-lives a quarter remains, after three an eighth.

misconceptions.question: Does the half-life change as a sample decays?
misconceptions.correct: No. The half-life of an isotope stays the same however much of the sample is left.
misconceptions.misconception: The half-life gets shorter, or the decay speeds up, as fewer nuclei remain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The count rate falls with time, which is read as the process changing rather than as fewer nuclei being available to decay.
misconceptions.correction: Each remaining nucleus always has the same chance of decaying in the next second, so the time to halve is always the same.

misconceptions.question: What is the net decline after 4 half-lives?
misconceptions.correct: A ratio of 1 : 16, because the emission halves four times.
misconceptions.misconception: After 4 half-lives the emission has fallen to a quarter, a ratio of 1 : 4.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number of half-lives is used directly as the dividing factor instead of as a power of 2.
misconceptions.correction: Halving four times divides by 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, so the ratio is 1 : 16.

misconceptions.question: Should a net decline be written 1 : 16 or 16 : 1?
misconceptions.correct: 1 : 16, comparing the final emission with the initial emission.
misconceptions.misconception: The ratio is written 16 : 1 because the activity has fallen sixteenfold.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The factor 16 is found correctly and then written first out of habit, without deciding which quantity each side stands for.
misconceptions.correction: A net decline compares what is left with what there was: final to initial. Sixteen times smaller is written 1 : 16.

misconceptions.question: Does an irradiated object become radioactive?
misconceptions.correct: No. Irradiation is exposure to radiation; the object does not become radioactive.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything exposed to a radioactive source becomes radioactive itself and stays dangerous afterwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radiation is pictured as a substance that soaks into things, like a dye or a smell.
misconceptions.correction: Radiation passes through or is absorbed, but leaves no radioactive atoms behind. Once the source is removed the object is safe.

misconceptions.question: What makes contamination hazardous?
misconceptions.correct: The decay of the contaminating atoms, which stay with the object and keep emitting radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: Contamination is only a hazard if the material can be seen or touched.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hazard is associated with contact, and contaminating dust is often invisible, so it is assumed to be harmless once out of sight.
misconceptions.correction: The hazard is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms. Invisible dust on skin, clothes or food keeps decaying wherever it is.

misconceptions.question: Is alpha radiation always the least dangerous?
misconceptions.correct: No. Outside the body it is easily blocked, but as a contaminant inside the body it is the most damaging.
misconceptions.misconception: Alpha is harmless in every situation because a sheet of paper stops it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The absorber table is memorised as a safety ranking, without asking where the source is.
misconceptions.correction: Inside the body there is no paper or skin in the way, and alpha's strong ionisation is all absorbed by nearby cells.

misconceptions.question: Which radiation is the greater hazard from a source inside the body?
misconceptions.correct: Alpha, because all of its strongly ionising energy is absorbed by the surrounding tissue.
misconceptions.misconception: Gamma is the greater hazard wherever the source is, because it goes through everything.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gamma is the more dangerous source outside the body, and that ranking is applied without change to a source inside it.
misconceptions.correction: Gamma mostly passes straight out of the body without being absorbed. Alpha deposits all its energy in a small volume of tissue.

misconceptions.question: What does peer review mean?
misconceptions.correct: Other scientists check published findings, repeating the analysis and looking for errors.
misconceptions.misconception: Peer review means the public or the government decides which results should be believed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Review' is associated with approval by an authority or with public opinion.
misconceptions.correction: Peer review is checking by other scientists with the expertise to repeat the work and spot mistakes in it.

misconceptions.question: Are precautions needed when a source is used to irradiate something?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Suitable precautions must be taken to protect against any hazard the source presents.
misconceptions.misconception: No precautions are needed, because the irradiated object does not become radioactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The safety of the irradiated object is confused with the safety of the people near the source.
misconceptions.correction: The object is safe, but the source itself keeps emitting. People are shielded from it, kept at a distance, and exposed for as short a time as possible.

misconceptions.question: Which source suits a smoke alarm?
misconceptions.correct: An alpha source, because alpha ionises the air strongly and is absorbed over a short range.
misconceptions.misconception: A gamma source is best because gamma is the most penetrating radiation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Most penetrating' is treated as 'best' for every job, without asking what the device needs to detect.
misconceptions.correction: The alarm works because smoke absorbs the radiation crossing a small gap. Gamma would pass through the smoke and the reading would not change.

misconceptions.question: Which source suits a gauge measuring the thickness of paper?
misconceptions.correct: A beta source, because the amount passing through changes as the thickness changes.
misconceptions.misconception: An alpha source is best because alpha ionises most strongly and gives the biggest signal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Strong ionisation is read as a strong reading, without asking whether any radiation reaches the detector at all.
misconceptions.correction: Paper stops alpha completely and barely affects gamma. Only beta is partly absorbed, so only beta gives a reading that varies with thickness.

misconceptions.question: Which source suits a medical tracer detected outside the body?
misconceptions.correct: A gamma source, because gamma passes out through the tissue to reach the detector.
misconceptions.misconception: An alpha source is best because alpha is the easiest radiation for a detector to pick up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alpha is remembered as the most ionising, so it is assumed to make the clearest signal in every arrangement.
misconceptions.correction: Alpha would be absorbed within a few centimetres of tissue, so nothing would reach the detector and the patient would receive the whole dose.

misconceptions.question: Does the nucleus store electrons ready to emit as beta particles?
misconceptions.correct: No. The electron is created as a neutron turns into a proton.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus contains electrons already, and beta decay simply lets one escape.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Ejected from the nucleus' is read as 'was already sitting in the nucleus'.
misconceptions.correction: There are no electrons in a nucleus. The beta particle comes into existence at the moment a neutron changes into a proton.

misconceptions.question: Do nuclei emit protons as one of the types of nuclear radiation?
misconceptions.correct: The specification lists alpha, beta, gamma and neutrons. A lone proton is not one of them.
misconceptions.misconception: Since a nucleus is made of protons and neutrons, it emits protons as a common form of radiation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Neutron emission is on the list, so the other nucleon is assumed to be emitted too.
misconceptions.correction: Protons leave only bound up in an alpha particle, which is two protons and two neutrons together.

misconceptions.question: How many times does the emission halve in 4 half-lives?
misconceptions.correct: Four times, giving a factor of 16.
misconceptions.misconception: Four half-lives means the 2 in halving multiplied by the 4, giving a factor of 8.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 2 in 'halving' and the 4 in 'four half-lives' are combined by multiplying instead of using 2 to the power 4.
misconceptions.correction: Each half-life multiplies the emission by 1/2, so four of them give 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2, which is 1/16.

misconceptions.question: Why are studies of radiation effects published?
misconceptions.correct: So the findings can be checked by other scientists through peer review.
misconceptions.misconception: Findings are published so the researchers get credit and further funding for their work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Publication is visible as a reward for scientists, so its role in checking the science is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Credit may follow, but the scientific purpose is that others can examine, repeat and challenge the findings before they are relied on.

mcqs.stem: A rock sample contains unstable nuclei. Which statement best describes radioactive decay?

options.text: An unstable nucleus gives out radiation at random as it changes to become more stable.
options.rationale: Matches the specification: unstable nuclei give out radiation as they become more stable, and the process is random.

options.text: Each unstable nucleus gives out its radiation at a time that can be predicted.
options.rationale: Half-lives are quoted as exact figures, so decay is pictured as scheduled rather than random.

options.text: A nucleus gives out radiation only after the rock has been heated strongly.
options.rationale: Every other rate met in science depends on temperature, so decay is assumed to as well.

options.text: Electrons dropping closer to the nucleus give out the radiation here.
options.rationale: Light emission by electrons changing energy level is transferred to radioactivity.

mcqs.stem: A teacher says that the activity of a source is falling. What does activity mean?

options.text: The number of decays a nearby detector records each second.
options.rationale: That is the count-rate; it is confused with activity because both are quoted per second.

options.text: The rate at which unstable nuclei in a source decay.
options.rationale: The specification defines activity as the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays.

options.text: The energy released by each decay in this source.
options.rationale: Activity is grouped with dose quantities, so it is read as an energy.

options.text: The time a source takes to lose half its nuclei.
options.rationale: Half-life is the best known number about a source, so it is offered for any definition.

mcqs.stem: The activity of a source is given as 480 Bq. What does the becquerel measure?

options.text: The energy the radiation from a source gives out each second.
options.rationale: Bq is grouped with the units used for dose, so it is read as an energy per second.

options.text: The number of counts a Geiger-Muller tube records each minute.
options.rationale: Count-rate is substituted for activity, and per minute for per second.

options.text: The number of decays that happen in a source each second.
options.rationale: One becquerel is one decay each second, so Bq measures activity.

options.text: The time taken for the activity of a source to halve.
options.rationale: Half-life is recalled instead, and given a unit that belongs to activity.

mcqs.stem: A student monitors a source with a Geiger-Muller tube. What is the count-rate?

options.text: The number of nuclei that decay in the whole source each second.
options.rationale: That is the activity; the detector is assumed to record every decay.

options.text: The energy given to the Geiger-Muller tube by radiation each second.
options.rationale: Counting events is confused with measuring the energy the tube absorbs.

options.text: The number of decays counted since the tube was switched on.
options.rationale: A running total is offered instead of a rate, so the word 'rate' is not read.

options.text: The number of decays recorded each second by the detector.
options.rationale: The specification's definition of count-rate exactly.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives the types of nuclear radiation that an unstable nucleus may emit?

options.text: Alpha particles, beta particles, X-rays and neutrons.
options.rationale: Gamma is replaced by X-rays because both are high energy electromagnetic radiation.

options.text: Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and neutrons.
options.rationale: These are the four emissions listed by the specification.

options.text: Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and protons.
options.rationale: If a neutron can be emitted, a proton is assumed to be emitted too.

options.text: Alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays only.
options.rationale: The familiar 'three radiations' is recalled and neutron emission is left out.

mcqs.stem: What is an alpha particle made of?

options.text: Two protons and two neutrons with two electrons in orbit around them.
options.rationale: 'Helium' is read as the whole atom rather than as the nucleus.

options.text: A single fast electron that has been thrown out of the nucleus.
options.rationale: The description of a beta particle is attached to alpha.

options.text: Two neutrons and two protons, which is the same as a helium nucleus.
options.rationale: The specification's own description of an alpha particle.

options.text: Two protons only, which is why the charge falls by two.
options.rationale: Only the protons are counted, which is the slip that makes the mass number fall by 2.

mcqs.stem: How do the properties of alpha radiation compare with those of beta and gamma?

options.text: It is the most penetrating radiation and travels furthest in air.
options.rationale: The largest, heaviest particle is assumed to push through the most material.

options.text: It is the least ionising but has the longest range in air.
options.rationale: Ionising power and penetration are assumed to rise together.

options.text: It ionises strongly and travels several metres through the air.
options.rationale: The ionising power is right but the range in air is taken to be metres.

options.text: It ionises most strongly and is stopped by a sheet of paper.
options.rationale: Alpha has the greatest ionising power, the shortest range in air and the least penetration.

mcqs.stem: What is a beta particle, and where does it come from?

options.text: A high speed electron ejected as a neutron turns into a proton.
options.rationale: The specification's own description of a beta particle.

options.text: A high speed electron knocked out of one of the outer electron shells.
options.rationale: Electrons are known as shell particles, so an emitted electron is assumed to be one.

options.text: An electron that had already been stored inside the nucleus itself.
options.rationale: 'Ejected from the nucleus' is read as 'was sitting in the nucleus'.

options.text: A high speed electron released as a proton turns into a neutron.
options.rationale: The change is reversed, which is the error that makes the atomic number fall.

mcqs.stem: A beta source is placed near a detector and different absorbers are tried. Which description of beta radiation is correct?

options.text: It is stopped by a sheet of paper and travels only a few centimetres.
options.rationale: The properties of alpha are attached to beta.

options.text: It ionises more strongly than an alpha particle and is stopped by card.
options.rationale: The ionising order is inverted, so beta is ranked above alpha.

options.text: It is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium and travels about a metre in air.
options.rationale: Beta's penetration and range in air, the two properties the specification requires.

options.text: It passes right through aluminium and is only reduced by thick lead.
options.rationale: The gamma row of the absorber table is attached to beta.

mcqs.stem: What is a gamma ray?

options.text: A heavy particle with no charge that is thrown out of the nucleus.
options.rationale: Gamma is listed with alpha and beta, so it is assumed to be a particle.

options.text: Radiation given out when an electron moves between two shells.
options.rationale: Emission by electrons changing energy level is transferred to the nucleus.

options.text: A fast moving particle carrying charge out of the nucleus.
options.rationale: The idea that everything emitted is a charged particle is carried over from alpha and beta.

options.text: Electromagnetic radiation given out from the nucleus of an atom.
options.rationale: The specification's own description of a gamma ray.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about gamma radiation is correct?

options.text: It is the least ionising radiation and the most penetrating one.
options.rationale: Gamma has the lowest ionising power, the greatest penetration and the longest range in air.

options.text: It is the most ionising radiation because it penetrates the furthest.
options.rationale: Penetration and ionising power are assumed to rise together.

options.text: It is completely absorbed by a thin sheet of lead or thin concrete.
options.rationale: 'Lead stops gamma' is memorised without the idea that gamma is only reduced.

options.text: It has the shortest range in air of the three radiations.
options.rationale: The ranges of alpha and gamma are swapped.

mcqs.stem: Some unstable nuclei emit a neutron. Which statement about this emission is correct?

options.text: A neutron cannot leave a nucleus, so this must really be beta decay.
options.rationale: Only three radiations are remembered, so a fourth is reinterpreted as beta.

options.text: A neutron (n) is one of the nuclear radiations a nucleus emits.
options.rationale: The specification lists a neutron (n) as one of the possible emissions.

options.text: The neutron carries a negative charge out of the nucleus with it.
options.rationale: Everything emitted is assumed to carry charge, as alpha and beta do.

options.text: Neutron emission is another name for the release of a gamma ray.
options.rationale: Both are uncharged, so the two emissions are treated as the same thing.

mcqs.stem: In a smoke alarm the radiation crosses a small gap in air and is absorbed when smoke enters the gap. Which source is best, and why?

options.text: Gamma, because it is the most penetrating and always reaches the sensor.
options.rationale: 'Most penetrating' is treated as best for any job, but gamma would pass through the smoke unchanged.

options.text: Beta, because it goes through smoke and is easy for a detector to see.
options.rationale: Passing through is valued, when the alarm depends on the smoke absorbing the radiation.

options.text: Gamma, because alpha would be far too dangerous to use in a home.
options.rationale: Alpha is judged dangerous in every situation, ignoring that it cannot escape the casing.

options.text: Alpha, because it ionises strongly and is absorbed over a short range in air.
options.rationale: Alpha's strong ionisation and few-centimetre range mean smoke in the gap changes the reading.

mcqs.stem: A paper mill measures the thickness of paper by detecting radiation that passes through it. Which source should be chosen?

options.text: Beta, because the amount getting through changes as the thickness changes.
options.rationale: Paper partly absorbs beta, so the count-rate responds to small changes in thickness.

options.text: Alpha, because it ionises most strongly and gives the largest reading of all.
options.rationale: Strong ionisation is read as a strong signal, but paper absorbs alpha completely.

options.text: Gamma, because it passes through the paper without being changed.
options.rationale: Penetration is valued for its own sake, but a reading that never changes is useless.

options.text: Alpha, because it is the safest radiation for the workers to be near.
options.rationale: Alpha is assumed harmless in all situations, and the measurement itself is forgotten.

mcqs.stem: A tracer is injected into a patient and its progress is followed by a detector held outside the body. Which source is most suitable?

options.text: An alpha emitter, because alpha ionises most and is the easiest to detect.
options.rationale: Strong ionisation is read as easy detection, but alpha never leaves the tissue.

options.text: A gamma emitter, because gamma passes out through the body tissue.
options.rationale: Only gamma is penetrating enough to leave the body and reach an external detector.

options.text: An alpha emitter, because paper stops alpha so it is harmless inside.
options.rationale: The absorber table is used as a safety ranking regardless of where the source is.

options.text: A beta emitter, because beta is stopped by skin and stays inside.
options.rationale: Being stopped is treated as an advantage, but nothing then reaches the detector.

mcqs.stem: In a nuclear equation, which symbol represents an alpha particle?

options.text: The symbol ²₄He, with the 2 written above the 4.
options.rationale: The mass number and the atomic number are written the wrong way round.

options.text: The symbol ⁰₋₁e, an electron from the nucleus.
options.rationale: The two decay symbols are confused with each other.

options.text: The symbol ⁴₂He, which is a helium nucleus.
options.rationale: The specification represents an alpha particle by ⁴₂He.

options.text: The symbol ¹₁H, which is a single proton leaving.
options.rationale: A lone proton is assumed to be emitted, so the proton symbol is chosen.

mcqs.stem: Which symbol is used for a beta particle in a nuclear equation?

options.text: ⁰₋₁e, so the mass number is 0 and the charge is −1.
options.rationale: The specification represents a beta particle by ⁰₋₁e.

options.text: ⁰₊₁e, so the mass number is 0 and charge is +1.
options.rationale: The rise in the charge of the nucleus is attached to the beta particle.

options.text: ¹₋₁e, giving a mass number of 1 and charge −1.
options.rationale: The emitted particle is assumed to carry a mass number of 1 away.

options.text: ¹₀n, so the mass number is 1 and charge 0.
options.rationale: The neutron symbol is chosen because a neutron is involved in beta decay.

mcqs.stem: A nucleus emits an alpha particle. How do its mass number and atomic number change?

options.text: The mass number falls by 2 and so does the atomic number.
options.rationale: Only the two protons are counted, so the two neutrons are missed.

options.text: The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.
options.rationale: Four nucleons leave, two of which are protons, so both mass and charge decrease.

options.text: The mass number falls by 4 but the atomic number does not.
options.rationale: The mass is tracked but the loss of two protons is not.

options.text: The mass number stays the same and the atomic number falls by 4.
options.rationale: The two numbers are swapped, so the change is applied to the wrong one.

mcqs.stem: A nucleus emits a beta particle. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?

options.text: The mass falls by 1 and the charge of the nucleus increases by 1.
options.rationale: A particle leaving is assumed to reduce the mass number.

options.text: The mass does not change and the charge of the nucleus falls by 1.
options.rationale: Losing a negative particle is read as losing charge.

options.text: The mass does not change but the charge increases by 1.
options.rationale: A neutron becomes a proton, so the nucleon count holds and the charge rises.

options.text: Both the mass and the charge of the nucleus fall by 1.
options.rationale: Both errors are combined: mass lost with the particle, charge lost with the minus sign.

mcqs.stem: When a nuclear equation for alpha decay is balanced, which quantities must be equal on both sides?

options.text: The number of protons only, as neutrons carry no charge.
options.rationale: Only charge is tracked, which is the slip that loses the neutrons in alpha decay.

options.text: The mass numbers only, as charge leaves with the alpha.
options.rationale: One number is balanced and the other is treated as simply lost.

options.text: The number of neutrons on each side of the equation.
options.rationale: Neutrons are counted directly instead of using the two numbers in the symbol.

options.text: The total mass number and the total atomic number.
options.rationale: Balancing is limited to making the mass numbers and the atomic numbers match.

mcqs.stem: Carbon-14 decays by beta emission: ¹⁴₆C → ᴬZ N + ⁰₋₁e. Which values of A and Z balance this equation?

options.text: A = 13 and Z = 7, since a particle has left the nucleus here.
options.rationale: The mass number is reduced because something was emitted.

options.text: A = 14 and Z = 7, since the charge rises as the mass stays the same.
options.rationale: Mass numbers 14 = 14 + 0 and atomic numbers 6 = 7 + (−1) both balance.

options.text: A = 14 and Z = 5, since a negative particle has been lost.
options.rationale: Losing a negative charge is read as the atomic number falling.

options.text: A = 13 and Z = 5, since both of the numbers must fall.
options.rationale: Both errors are combined and both numbers are reduced.

mcqs.stem: A nucleus emits a gamma ray. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?

options.text: The mass number falls a little because energy has been carried off.
options.rationale: Emitting something is assumed to reduce the mass number.

options.text: The charge increases by one but the mass number is the same.
options.rationale: The beta decay result is applied to gamma emission.

options.text: Neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus is changed at all.
options.rationale: A gamma ray has no mass number and no charge, so both numbers are unchanged.

options.text: The mass number falls by four and the charge falls by two.
options.rationale: The alpha decay result is applied to gamma emission.

mcqs.stem: Which statement shows that radioactive decay is a random process?

options.text: Each nucleus in the sample decays exactly one half-life after the last.
options.rationale: Half-life is read as a timetable that individual nuclei follow in turn.

options.text: The decay of the sample speeds up as the number of nuclei drops.
options.rationale: The falling count rate is read as the process itself changing.

options.text: Decay can be started or stopped by heating up the sample.
options.rationale: Decay is treated as a chemical rate that conditions can control.

options.text: It is impossible to say which nucleus will decay next, or when.
options.rationale: Unpredictability of the individual event is exactly what randomness means here.

mcqs.stem: The half-life of an isotope is 6 hours. What does this tell you about a sample of it?

options.text: In 6 hours the count rate from the sample halves.
options.rationale: The specification defines half-life by the count rate or activity falling to half its initial level.

options.text: In 6 hours every nucleus in the sample will have decayed.
options.rationale: 'Life' is read as a lifetime, so the sample is thought to be finished.

options.text: In 12 hours the sample will contain no unstable nuclei.
options.rationale: Two halves are added to make a whole instead of applied one after the other.

options.text: In 6 hours half of the mass of the sample disappears.
options.rationale: The number of undecayed nuclei is confused with the mass of material present.

mcqs.stem: If the decay of each nucleus is random, why does a sample have a definite half-life?

options.text: Because each nucleus waits its turn, so the decays are evenly spread out.
options.rationale: Randomness is replaced by an orderly queue that produces the smooth curve.

options.text: Because every nucleus is timed to decay after the same fixed period.
options.rationale: A definite half-life is read as a definite lifetime for each nucleus.

options.text: Because a sample holds so many nuclei that their average behaviour is predictable.
options.rationale: Large numbers make the statistics reliable even though each single event is unpredictable.

options.text: Because half of the nuclei are unstable and the other half are stable.
options.rationale: The 'half' in half-life is attached to the make-up of the sample.

mcqs.stem: The count rate from a source falls from 800 counts per second to 100 counts per second in 24 minutes. What is the half-life?

options.text: 24 minutes: only one halving takes place
options.rationale: The whole time is quoted as the half-life without counting the halvings.

options.text: 12 minutes: half of the total time
options.rationale: 'Half' is applied to the time interval instead of to the count rate.

options.text: 6 minutes: 800 falls to 100 in four
options.rationale: One halving too many is counted, giving 24 divided by 4.

options.text: 8 minutes: three halvings take place
options.rationale: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100 is three halvings in 24 minutes, so each takes 8 minutes.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) The emission from a source is measured, and measured again after 4 half-lives have passed. What is the net decline, expressed as a ratio?

options.text: 1 : 16, as the emission halves four times over
options.rationale: Four halvings divide the emission by 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, written 1 : 16.

options.text: 1 : 4, as there are four half-lives in total here
options.rationale: The number of half-lives is used as the dividing factor instead of as a power of 2.

options.text: 16 : 1, since the emission is now sixteen times less
options.rationale: The factor is right but the ratio is written the wrong way round.

options.text: 1 : 8, from doubling the four half-lives here
options.rationale: The 2 and the 4 are multiplied instead of using 2 to the power 4.

mcqs.stem: A worker finds radioactive dust on their overalls. Which statement describes the situation correctly?

options.text: This is contamination, but it is only a hazard if the dust can be seen.
options.rationale: Hazard is tied to being visible, when the decay continues either way.

options.text: This is contamination; the hazard is the decay of the dust.
options.rationale: Contamination is the unwanted presence of radioactive atoms, and the hazard is their decay.

options.text: This is irradiation, and the overalls have now become radioactive.
options.rationale: The two terms are swapped and exposure is assumed to make things radioactive.

options.text: This is contamination, and the dust is a hazard by touch alone.
options.rationale: The hazard is attributed to contact rather than to the radiation emitted.

mcqs.stem: Fruit is exposed to gamma radiation from a source in order to kill bacteria on it. What happens to the fruit?

options.text: The fruit becomes radioactive and must be stored before it is sold.
options.rationale: Radiation is pictured as soaking in and staying, like a dye.

options.text: The fruit becomes contaminated with atoms from the gamma source.
options.rationale: Irradiation is confused with contamination by radioactive material.

options.text: The fruit is irradiated, so no precautions are needed by workers.
options.rationale: The safety of the fruit is confused with the safety of people near the source.

options.text: The fruit has been irradiated; it does not become radioactive itself.
options.rationale: Irradiation is exposure to radiation, and the irradiated object does not become radioactive.

mcqs.stem: Why is an alpha emitter more hazardous inside the body than outside it?

options.text: Inside, its strong ionisation is absorbed by cells; outside, skin stops it.
options.rationale: Contamination puts the alpha source past the skin, where all of its ionising energy is absorbed.

options.text: It is never a hazard inside, because a sheet of paper is able to stop alpha.
options.rationale: The absorber table is used as a safety ranking regardless of where the source sits.

options.text: Gamma is worse inside the body, because it passes through everything.
options.rationale: The outside-the-body ranking is applied unchanged to a source inside it.

options.text: Alpha is only a hazard if the source is touched with bare hands.
options.rationale: The hazard is attributed to contact rather than to the decay of the atoms.

mcqs.stem: A technician uses a gamma source to irradiate surgical equipment. Which precaution is appropriate?

options.text: None is needed, because irradiated objects do not become radioactive.
options.rationale: The safety of the object is confused with the hazard the source still presents.

options.text: Handle the source with tongs and store it in a lead-lined box.
options.rationale: Distance and shielding protect against the hazard the source used for irradiation presents.

options.text: Wear a paper mask, since paper is able to absorb gamma radiation.
options.rationale: Paper absorbs alpha, not gamma; the rows of the absorber table are muddled.

options.text: Rinse the equipment afterwards to wash the radioactivity off.
options.rationale: The equipment is assumed to have become radioactive during irradiation.

mcqs.stem: Studies of the effects of radiation on humans are published and shared with other scientists. Why does this matter?

options.text: So that members of the public can vote on whether the work is right.
options.rationale: 'Review' is read as approval by popular opinion rather than by experts.

options.text: So that the government decides which findings should be believed.
options.rationale: Checking is assumed to be done by an authority rather than by scientists.

options.text: So that other scientists check the findings by peer review.
options.rationale: The specification requires findings to be shared so they can be checked by peer review.

options.text: So that the researchers are paid for all of the work they did.
options.rationale: Publication is seen as a reward for scientists rather than as a check on the science.
